column7: I'm going shopping this evening.
column8: German supermarkets close early and stay closed almost every Sunday, which surprises visitors from Mediterranean countries.

column7: I'll call you tomorrow.

column6: Sie fährt jeden Tag mit dem Fahrrad.

column6: In meiner Freizeit spiele ich Gitarre.

column6: Die deutsche Küche ist sehr vielfältig.

column7: He likes eating fish.
column8: The irregular 'isst' from 'essen' is an e→i shift, one of German's most productive patterns, shared by verbs like 'geben' and 'sprechen'.

column7: We're going on vacation to Italy.
column8: Germany is among the world's top spenders on tourism, and Italy has long been Germans' favorite destination.

column6: Das Krankenhaus ist in der Stadtmitte.

column7: My colleague always helps me.

column7: I'm tidying my room.
column8: 'Aufräumen' is separable: 'ich räume auf', Perfekt 'hat aufgeräumt'.

column6: Können wir bitte die Rechnung haben?
column7: Can we have the bill, please?
column8: At German restaurants you're often asked 'zusammen oder getrennt?' ('together or separate?') — splitting the bill is entirely normal.

column7: I'm preparing the meal.
column8: The prefix 'vor-' (before, in front) generates dozens of separable verbs like 'vorschlagen' (to suggest) and 'vorstellen' (to introduce).

column6: Ich habe morgen einen Termin beim Zahnarzt.
column7: I have a dentist appointment tomorrow.

column7: Our neighbour is very friendly.
column8: German apartment buildings have 'Ruhezeit': quiet hours after 10pm and often all of Sunday. Neighbours take it seriously.

column6: Bring bitte etwas zu trinken mit.
column7: Please bring something to drink.
column8: At a party in Germany you usually bring something: showing up empty-handed can seem impolite.

column6: Am Sonntag machen wir einen Ausflug an den See.

column8: The Sunday nature outing is a German classic, often combined with a stop at a countryside 'Gasthaus'.

column7: My head hurts.

column6: Das Gehalt wird am Monatsende gezahlt.
column7: The salary is paid at the end of the month.

column6: Zieh dir eine Jacke an, es ist kalt.

column8: The opposite is 'ausziehen' (to take off): the prefix pair 'an-/aus-' works like on/off.

column6: Wir kaufen neue Möbel für die Wohnung.

column6: Wir treffen uns um sieben vor dem Kino.

column6: Ich muss für die Prüfung lernen.

column8: The suffix '-ung' makes almost every noun it forms feminine, often starting from a verb ('prüfen' → 'Prüfung').

column7: In Munich we have to change trains.

column6: Ich suche ein Geschenk für meine Mutter.

column6: Kannst du mir das noch einmal erklären?

column7: We're looking for a bigger apartment.

column6: Ich lade dich zum Essen ein.

column6: Das war mein Fehler, es tut mir leid.

column7: Fruit and vegetables are healthy.

column6: Wir steigen an der nächsten Haltestelle aus.

column7: We're moving next month.

column7: Please close the window.

column7: Can you open the door?

column7: Would you like to come along?

column8: 'Mitnehmen' takes a direct accusative object for the thing carried along, with no extra preposition needed.

column7: I'll be back at six.
column8: 'Zurückkommen' uses 'sein' in the Perfekt like all compounds of 'kommen', indicating movement.

column6: Ich gebe dir das Buch morgen zurück.

column6: Komm doch mal bei uns vorbei.

column6: Der Film fängt um acht an.

column8: 'Anfangen' and 'beginnen' are near-synonyms, but 'anfangen' is more colloquial and common in everyday speech.

column6: Er hört nicht mit dem Rauchen auf.

column7: We're going out tonight.

column6: Ich nehme an dem Kurs teil.

column6: Ich erinnere mich an meine Kindheit.

column6: Die Scheidung war für alle schwer.
column7: The divorce was hard on everyone.
column8: 'Scheidung' comes from 'scheiden' (to separate, to part), the same verb used for 'Abschied' (farewell).

column6: Das Paar wohnt seit Jahren zusammen.
column7: The couple has lived together for years.
column8: Lowercase 'ein paar' means 'a few', while capitalized 'ein Paar' means 'a couple/pair' — the capital letter changes the meaning.

column7: My partner is from France.
column8: 'Partner' is a gender-neutral term, used for boyfriends/girlfriends, spouses, or life partners in general.

column7: We're celebrating our engagement.
column8: 'Verlobung' comes from 'sich verloben' (to get formally engaged), a formal step preceding marriage.

column6: Unsere Freundschaft dauert schon zwanzig Jahre.
column7: Our friendship has already lasted twenty years.
column8: 'Freundschaft schließen' ('to forge a friendship') is the standard fixed collocation for starting a friendship.

column7: They have a good relationship.
column8: 'Beziehung' comes from 'beziehen' (to relate to): the concept of a connection between two people or things.

column6: Vertrauen ist die Basis jeder Beziehung.
column7: Trust is the foundation of every relationship.
column8: 'Vertrauen' is both a noun and the nominalized infinitive of the verb 'vertrauen' (to trust), which takes the dative.

column7: They had an argument yesterday.
column8: 'Streit haben' is the standard structure for talking about an argument, while 'streiten' is the corresponding verb.

column6: Sie haben sich schnell wieder versöhnt.
column7: They quickly made up again.
column8: 'Sich versöhnen' isn't separable: it belongs to the group of verbs with the inseparable prefix 'ver-'.

column7: That was just a misunderstanding.
column8: 'Missverständnis' combines the negative prefix 'miss-' with 'Verständnis' (understanding): literally 'non-understanding'.

column6: Kannst du ein Geheimnis für dich behalten?
column7: Can you keep a secret to yourself?
column8: 'Für sich behalten' ('to keep to oneself') is the fixed expression for saying something will stay confidential.

column7: That was a small lie.
column8: 'Lügen haben kurze Beine' ('lies have short legs') matches the English 'lies have short legs' almost exactly.

column7: Please tell me the truth.
column8: 'Die Wahrheit sagen' takes a direct accusative object with no preposition — the most common standard structure.

column7: He has a calm character.
column8: 'Charakter' describes a person's personality, different from 'Figur', which means 'character' in a novel or film.

column7: The shop assistant was very friendly.
column8: 'Freundlich' shares a root with 'Freund' (friend), an adjective describing an open attitude toward others.

column6: Sei bitte höflich zu den Gästen.
column7: Please be polite to the guests.
column8: 'Höflich' comes from 'Hof' (court): it originally described behavior appropriate to a royal court.

column6: Ehrlich gesagt, ich weiß es nicht.
column7: Honestly, I don't know.
column8: 'Ehrlich gesagt' ('honestly said') is one of the most common opening phrases for giving an honest opinion.

column7: My teacher is very patient.
column8: 'Geduldig' derives from 'Geduld' (patience) with the adjectival suffix '-ig', very productive in German.

column6: Kinder sind von Natur aus neugierig.
column7: Children are naturally curious.
column8: 'Neugierig' combines 'neu' (new) and 'gierig' (greedy): literally 'greedy for new things'.

column6: Er ist sehr großzügig mit seiner Zeit.
column7: He's very generous with his time.
column8: 'Großzügig' combines 'groß' (big) and 'Zug' (trait/pull): literally 'of great traits', i.e. magnanimous.

column6: Als Kind war ich sehr schüchtern.
column7: As a child I was very shy.
column8: 'Schüchtern' describes shy people and behaviour: 'ein schüchterner Junge', 'schüchtern lächeln'.

column7: That was a brave decision.
column8: 'Mutig' comes from 'Mut' (courage) with the suffix '-ig', one of the most regular patterns of German adjective formation.

column6: Am Wochenende bin ich manchmal faul.
column7: On weekends I'm sometimes lazy.
column8: 'Faul' also means 'rotten, spoiled' when referring to food — two distinct meanings from the same word.

column6: Sie ist eine sehr fleißige Studentin.
column7: She's a very hardworking student.
column8: 'Fleißig' is the direct opposite of 'faul' and is often used to compliment dedicated students.

column7: My colleague is very reliable.
column8: 'Zuverlässig' combines 'zu' and 'verlassen' (to rely on): literally 'that which one can lean on'.

column6: Deutsche Züge sind nicht immer pünktlich.
column7: German trains aren't always punctual.
column8: Despite the stereotype of German punctuality, rail delays have become a frequent topic of debate in recent years.

column7: His behavior was quite selfish.
column8: 'Egoistisch' is a loanword from French/Latin, integrated with the normal German adjectival ending '-isch'.

column7: He gets jealous quickly.
column8: 'Eifersüchtig' combines 'Eifer' (zeal, fervor) and 'süchtig' (addicted): literally 'afflicted with excessive zeal'.

column6: Ich war total überrascht von der Party.
column7: I was totally surprised by the party.
column8: 'Überrascht sein von' takes the dative: 'von der Party', used to express surprise at something specific.

column6: Ich bin von dem Ergebnis enttäuscht.
column7: I'm disappointed with the result.
column8: 'Enttäuscht' is the past participle of 'enttäuschen' (to disappoint), used as an adjective with 'von' plus the dative.

column6: Sie ist begeistert von der Reise.
column7: She's enthusiastic about the trip.
column8: 'Begeistert von' takes the dative, the same structure used by 'enttäuscht' and 'überrascht'.

column7: The instructions confused me.
column8: 'Verwirrt' comes from 'verwirren' (to confuse), an inseparable verb with the prefix 'ver-'.

column7: The children were bored.
column8: 'Gelangweilt' is a participle used as an adjective: it describes how you feel ('ich bin gelangweilt'). 'Langweilig' describes what causes it: 'der Film ist langweilig'.

column6: Ich bin mit meiner Arbeit zufrieden.
column7: I'm satisfied with my work.
column8: 'Zufrieden mit' takes the dative: 'mit meiner Arbeit' — a common structure for expressing satisfaction.

column6: Vor der Prüfung bin ich immer nervös.
column7: Before the exam I'm always nervous.
column8: 'Nervös' is a loanword from French, stressed on the last syllable, unlike many native German adjectives.

column7: He got quite embarrassed.
column8: 'Verlegen' as an adjective is different from 'verlegen' as a verb (to move, to mislay) — same form, different meanings depending on context.

column6: Ich bin dir sehr dankbar für deine Hilfe.
column7: I'm very grateful to you for your help.
column8: 'Dankbar für' takes the accusative: 'für deine Hilfe', while 'dankbar' alone can also take the dative of the person.

column7: I have a strange feeling.
column8: 'Gefühl' comes from 'fühlen' (to feel), with the collective prefix 'ge-' typical of many abstract neuter nouns.

column7: She's in a good mood today.
column8: 'Gute Laune haben' and 'schlechte Laune haben' are the standard structures for talking about everyday mood.

column7: He has a strong personality.
column8: 'Persönlichkeit' comes from 'Person' with the double suffix '-lich' plus '-keit', creating a complex abstract noun.

column6: Ich habe die Gewohnheit, früh aufzustehen.
column7: I have the habit of getting up early.
column8: 'Die Gewohnheit haben, ... zu' takes the infinitive with 'zu' — a common structure for describing personal routines.

column6: Ich gewöhne mich langsam an das Klima.
column7: I'm slowly getting used to the climate.
column8: 'Sich gewöhnen an' always takes the accusative: 'an das Klima' — a very common fixed structure.

column7: I miss my family a lot.
column8: Unlike 'fehlen' (which uses the dative with an inverted subject), 'vermissen' works like English 'to miss': it takes a direct accusative object.

column7: Italy is my homeland.
column8: 'Heimat' carries deep emotional weight in German, tied to a sense of belonging rather than the mere geographic idea of 'country'.

column6: Sprache ist ein Teil der Identität.
column7: Language is part of identity.
column8: 'Identität' is nearly identical across many European languages, one of many learned Latin loanwords they share.

column6: Die deutsche Kultur ist sehr vielfältig.
column7: German culture is very diverse.
column8: 'Kultur' is the root of 'Kulturschock' (culture shock), a term widely used among people living abroad.

column6: Diese Tradition wird seit Generationen gepflegt.
column7: This tradition has been kept alive for generations.
column8: 'Pflegen' means both 'to nurture, maintain' a tradition and 'to physically care for' someone who is sick.

column6: Die Vielfalt der Dialekte ist beeindruckend.
column7: The diversity of dialects is impressive.
column8: Germany has dozens of regional dialects that differ greatly, some almost incomprehensible to speakers of only standard German.

column6: In Bayern spricht man oft Dialekt.
column7: In Bavaria, people often speak in dialect.
column8: Bavarian, Saxon, and Cologne dialect are among the most distinctive German dialects, often hard for standard-German learners to follow.

column6: In der Schule lernt man Hochdeutsch.
column7: At school you learn Standard German.
column8: 'Hochdeutsch' literally means 'high German', a historical term tied to geography rather than a value judgment.

column6: Nach dem Regen kam ein Regenbogen.
column7: After the rain a rainbow appeared.
column8: 'Regenbogen' is a transparent compound: 'Regen' (rain) + 'Bogen' (arc/bow), literally a 'rain arc'.

column7: I'd like to make an appointment.
column8: 'Vereinbaren' isn't separable: it belongs to the group of verbs with the always-inseparable prefix 'ver-'.

column6: Wir haben uns in der Stadt verlaufen.
column7: We got lost in the city.
column8: 'Sich verlaufen' describes getting lost on foot; 'sich verfahren' is the equivalent for getting lost while driving.

column7: Please check the mailbox.
column8: 'Briefkasten' = 'Brief' (letter) + 'Kasten' (box): both the one at home and the yellow one in the street.

column6: Das Mädchen spielt mit dem Ball im Garten.
column7: The girl is playing with the ball in the garden.
column8: Although the person is female, the word is neuter: the suffix '-chen' makes any noun neuter. The article stays 'das'.

column6: Meine Eltern wohnen in einer kleinen Stadt.
column7: My parents live in a small town.
column8: 'Eltern' exists only in the plural; for one parent say 'Elternteil', 'Vater' or 'Mutter'. Note that 'Verwandte' means relatives, not parents.

column6: Meine Tochter geht schon in die Schule.
column7: My daughter already goes to school.
column8: The plural takes an umlaut: 'Töchter'. The masculine is 'Sohn' (plural 'Söhne').

column6: Unser Sohn spielt am Samstag Fußball.
column7: Our son plays soccer on Saturday.
column8: The plural takes an umlaut: 'Söhne'. For 'child' without specifying sex, use 'Kind'.

column6: Vielleicht gehen wir morgen ins Kino.
column7: Maybe we will go to the cinema tomorrow.
column8: It often opens the sentence and the verb follows right after (verb in second position). It also softens requests: 'Könnten Sie vielleicht helfen?'.

column6: Manchmal esse ich abends nur Brot.
column7: Sometimes I only eat bread in the evening.
column8: A frequency adverb between 'nie' and 'oft'. Do not mix it up with 'manche' (some), which is a pronoun or adjective.

column7: Please come home right away!
column8: 'Sofort' means with no delay and is stronger than 'gleich' (in a moment). Synonym: 'auf der Stelle'.

column7: We will see each other again soon.
column8: 'Bald' looks to the near future. Farewell phrase: 'Bis bald!'. Do not confuse it with 'früh' (early in the day or ahead of time).

column6: Leider habe ich heute keine Zeit.
column7: Unfortunately I have no time today.
column8: 'Leider' expresses the speaker's regret and is often used to decline politely. The adjective 'leid' appears in 'Es tut mir leid'.

column7: I still need ten minutes.
column8: 'Brauchen' takes the accusative. With 'nicht brauchen' + 'zu' + infinitive it means 'not have to': 'Du brauchst nicht zu kommen'.

column7: I am getting a package tomorrow.
column8: A false friend: 'bekommen' does not mean 'become' (that is 'werden') but 'receive'. Its participle is 'bekommen', with no 'ge-'.

column7: I often forget my key.
column8: Irregular: 'er vergisst', Perfekt 'hat vergessen'. You can say 'etwas vergessen' or 'vergessen zu' + infinitive.

column6: Ich versuche, jeden Tag Deutsch zu sprechen.
column7: I try to speak German every day.
column8: It often takes 'zu' + infinitive with a comma. It also does not mean 'taste': for food use 'probieren'.

column6: Was bedeutet dieses Wort auf Italienisch?
column7: What does this word mean in Italian?
column8: 'Bedeuten' is regular and inseparable: 'hat bedeutet'. The noun is 'Bedeutung'. 'Meinen' refers to what a speaker intends.

column6: Es regnet, deshalb bleiben wir zu Hause.
column7: It is raining, so we are staying at home.
column8: After 'deshalb' the verb comes right next (position 2): it is not a subordinating conjunction. Synonym: 'deswegen'.

column6: Das ist kein Tee, sondern Kaffee.
column7: That is not tea but coffee.
column8: 'Sondern' is used only after a negation and corrects it: 'not A, but B'. For a contrast without correction use 'aber'.

column7: The weekend is finally here!
column8: 'Endlich' expresses relief after a long wait. Do not confuse it with 'schließlich' (in the end) or 'endgültig' (final).
